settings.content: Could I even put anything on my face while I was still feeding him? A hundred and fifty-nine women asked that — more than any other question in three thousand — and under it, every time, the same fear: that a cream on her face could reach her baby. That fear isn't irrational. It's love doing its job — it was doing its job in me, hard.

I can't answer it for you, and I want to be exact about why. Not legal caution — I don't know you, I don't know your baby, and I'm not your OB. One woman put the objection better than I could, and she was talking about companies exactly like the one I'd end up building:

settings.quote: "I don't trust when companies say that it may be safe. They don't know YOUR body."

settings.content: She's right, and that ends the argument. So here is what I can do instead of arguing with her.

The most-recommended ingredient across every community I read was azelaic acid — not by us, by them, to each other, for years. The US National Library of Medicine runs a lactation database. On topical azelaic acid it records that roughly four percent is absorbed, and that it is not a reason to stop breastfeeding.

settings.text: That's their sentence, not ours. It's public, it's free, and it took me under a minute to find.

settings.content: That's what made me angry, four days in. Not that the answer was complicated — that it was one search away, and a hundred and fifty-nine women asked into the dark anyway. The other five follow the same rule: centella, colloidal oat, panthenol, licochalcone, a low-dose niacinamide — all topical and local, none a systemic drug. Don't take my word for it. I'm going to put the whole list in your hand so you can ask with it.
And then there was the harder version of the question — the one I heard from a woman who'd already been to her dermatologist:

settings.quote: "My derm says nothing can be done until I stop breastfeeding. I hate to stop breastfeeding to control my rosacea."

settings.content: It looks like choosing your face over your baby. It isn't. It's a false choice, handed to her by someone with six minutes, then left in her lap. Some of it's true — several strong prescriptions genuinely do wait until you've weaned. But nothing can be done and I can't give you the strong thing today are not the same sentence, and only one of them was said to her.

settings.text: Nobody should be weaning a baby to fix a cheek.
Two honest limits, while I'm here: not for sore or gritty eyelids — that wants an eye doctor, this week — and not in the first six weeks after birth; your skin has enough happening.

settings.content: Which leaves one last question. I almost left it out, because only eight women in three thousand were brave enough to type it. It's the one I'd read nine hundred posts before I understood.
